lesson.title: Two Paths to the Same Distance: Solving Absolute Value Equations
lesson.summary: Absolute value equations ask which numbers sit a fixed distance from zero, so solving them usually means splitting one equation into two ordinary linear equations.
lesson.body:
Every absolute value bar is a distance instruction. When you write |x|, you are asking how far x is from zero on the number line, and that distance is always zero or positive, never negative. So when an equation reads |x| = 5, it is really asking a question in disguise: which numbers are exactly 5 units from zero? There are exactly two answers, 5 and negative 5, because you can walk 5 steps to the right or 5 steps to the left and land the same distance away. This is the entire idea behind absolute value equations: a single equation with bars usually hides two separate linear equations, and solving it means uncovering both.

The general rule is that if |expression| = a and a is a positive number, then expression = a or expression = negative a. Before applying that rule, you need the absolute value expression completely alone on one side of the equation, the same isolating work you already practice in solving equations. Once it is isolated, drop the bars and write two equations, one where the inside equals a, and one where the inside equals the opposite of a. Each of those two equations is then solved using ordinary algebra, the same steps you already know from balancing equations with addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

Here is a full example. Solve |2x - 3| = 7. The absolute value is already isolated, so split it into two cases. Case one: 2x - 3 = 7. Adding 3 to both sides gives 2x = 10, and dividing by 2 gives x = 5. Case two: 2x - 3 = -7. Adding 3 to both sides gives 2x = -4, and dividing by 2 gives x = -2. Now check both answers in the original equation. For x = 5: |2(5) - 3| = |10 - 3| = |7| = 7, which matches. For x = -2: |2(-2) - 3| = |-4 - 3| = |-7| = 7, which also matches. Both solutions check out, so the full solution set is x = 5 or x = -2.

Two special situations are worth watching for. If the number on the other side of the equation is negative, there is no solution at all, because an absolute value can never equal a negative number. For instance, |x + 1| = -3 has no solution, no matter what x is, since the left side can never go below zero. If the number on the other side is exactly zero, the two cases collapse into one, giving a single solution instead of two. For example, |x + 1| = 0 only works when x + 1 = 0, so x = -1 is the only answer.

Sometimes the absolute value is not alone at the start, and you must isolate it first, just like isolating a variable. To solve 3|x| + 2 = 11, subtract 2 from both sides to get 3|x| = 9, then divide by 3 to get |x| = 3, and only now split into x = 3 or x = -3. Skipping the isolation step and splitting too early is one of the most common mistakes, so always get the bars alone before removing them. This same two-case thinking is the foundation for absolute value inequalities, where the same splitting idea applies but the direction of the answer changes depending on the inequality symbol involved.
